entry.title: How to find the tomb in PEAK
entry.summary:
PEAK's Mesa biome has plenty of mysteries littered across the region, and one such area is the tomb, which can be pretty easy to miss.
This place, like the capybara spawn location, is entirely random, but it is much harder to spot. This guide will help you clear your doubts about the place, including certain features that appear, and bugs (the software type, not the insects).
Table of contents How to locate the tomb in PEAK? How to access the tomb in PEAK?
How to locate the tomb in PEAK?
The tomb's exact location might be random, but it's always located in the first part of the Mesa biome. If you don't want to move around aimlessly, I recommend using the game's official Discord server. It's the largest PEAK community on social media, and other players will be more than willing to help you out.
While the exact location of the tomb varies daily, they appear at the same spot on every seed. This makes it relatively easy to find the elusive spot. If you still want to give it a try, you can always try to find the place on your own. Make sure to use items like Aloe Vera and Sunscreen to combat the heat.
Screenshot by Destructoid
How to access the tomb in PEAK?
Once you reach the correct location, look for a hole within a rocky outcropping. Typically, they're easier to spot from a height. However, the entrance isn't high itself, and goes deep into the underground.
The tomb won't be open on all days. This is part of the design mechanism. You can use a mod to bypass this limitation, but you can avoid that if you want to stay squeaky clean.
Once inside, navigate the lean path and make your way to the spot where you'll find the Ancient Idol. This Idol itself can protect you from certain hazards, but it's better to throw it into the lava to complete one of the hardest badges in the entire game.
The post How to find the tomb in PEAK appeared first on Destructoid.

Masahiro Sakurai is celebrating the 20th anniversary of his company, Sora, and casually dropped that we might be getting new Kirby Air Riders information out of nowhere.
We haven't seen any gameplay or much news about the new Kirby game since its initial reveal halfway through the year during the Switch 2 game presentation. Although the title is expected to release sometime this year, there is no news of a release date or information about the gameplay at all.

When that soon is, though, remains a mystery, but there is one big event happening next week where we might expect to see something revealed—Gamescom.
Nintendo doesn't usually reveal big games during Opening Night Live and usually retains information for its own direct, so while a big Nintendo Direct sometime this month might not be out of the question, Sakurai is a fan of having his own presentations and Nintendo Directs with previous titles like Super Smash Bros. Ultimate, so maybe we get a whole direct dedicated to Kirby Air Riders soon?
It's all speculation, of course.
Kirby Air Riders is the sequel to the 2003 GameCube title Kirby Air Ride, a racing game set in the Kirby universe where players control different colored Kirbys through various vehicle-based races. By the looks of the initial trailer, the new game seems to follow that premise, but we still have a lot of questions about the direction the game will take. It would also be the second big Nintendo racing IP on the Nintendo Switch 2, following the launch of Mario Kart World.

entry.title: Review: UFO 50 (Switch) - A Wondrous Smorgasbord Of Retro Delights
entry.summary: I want to believe. While playing UFO 50 for this review, I visited an exhibition at London’s Science Museum: Power Up – a hands-on tour of the last five decades of video games. There, in an expansive, dark basement, an orange-illuminated wall of computers and consoles took me right through the 1980s. I sampled such delicacies as a flickery Chuckie Egg on the BBC Micro, an Asteroids-type game on the Vectrex, and Metroid on the NES. It was like an 8-bit time machine, beep-blooping me into any year I fancied, to have a little taste of what was there. UFO 50 is just like that – except the time machine has taken a wrong turn and ended up in a parallel universe. Here, a pioneering (fictional) company, UFO Soft, produced a snazzy home console called the Lazer-X, then prolifically churned out games for it over eight years from 1982 to 1989. The IRL developers – a group of six indie devs at Mossmouth (Derek Yu’s studio behind Spelunky) – calling themselves the “UFO 50 Recovery Team”, unearthed this machine. How strange it is that something so new (at least in the context it’s being presented) can feel so inescapably ancient. If you get a relative or mate who’s unfamiliar with the Mafia series to play Hangar 13’s latest work, I’m fairly convinced that you’ll have an easier time convincing them that they’d just sampled a remaster of a game from the 2000s than a new release from 2025. entry.title: Folk Emerging is a fascinating 4X strategy game about prehistoric nomads that ends where Civilization begins
entry.summary:
Folk Emerging describes itself as a turn-based 4X strategy game, but in practice, it's possibly more of a 2.5X strategy game, in that it puts you in charge of a nomadic hunter-gatherer community from before the rise of agriculture and the founding of towns and cities.
As this developer update suggests, it's like the turn or two at the very start of Civilization when you just have one Settler unit, but stretched out across thousands of years, with a social element and rustic spreadsheet aesthetics that remind me of King Of Dragon Pass. It's got somewhat doofy cartoon Stone Age muzak, but is otherwise the most intriguing Civlike strategy game I've laid eyes on since the one that looks like an octopus murder scene - and whadayaknow, by happy coincidence there's a public playtest running from right now till August 18th.

entry.title: Apex Legends' latest go at a compressed battle royale forgets the journeying spirit at the genre's heart
entry.summary: Apex Legends launched its Season 26 update this week with the new Wildcard mode, what must be its fourth or fifth attempt at a 'battle royale but faster' sideshow. If anything, Wildcard – with its tightened safe zones, generous respawn allowances and automatic loot pickups – is the most ferocious, cage fightin'est variant yet, its matches routinely playing out as breathless slaughters as crammed-in squads fight, die, and resurrect over a condensed selection of strongholds. Still, while I’ve enjoyed ApeLegs' previous action-favouring tweaks, something about Wildcard underwhelms. It’s not the shooting, which is as crisp and dynamic as in any other Respawn FPS. And it’s not the simplified gear gobbling, which is fine for a supplementary mode. It’s that at the end of a Wildcard round, even the ones I’ve won, I’ve never felt that I’ve really gone anywhere or done anything except aim down my sights and left-click. In chasing nonstop drama it denies you something that good battle royales, and their progenitors, can so effectively deliver: a journey. Read more

entry.title: Audio recenze: Fantastická 4: První kroky [The Fantastic Four: First Steps] - 50 %
entry.summary: Prvních přibližně 20 minut jsem byl skoro nadšený. Mělo to švih, krásnou retrofuturistickou výpravu, bylo to (záměrně!) mírně debilní jako sci-fi z 50. let, ale... Pak většina z toho zmizela (včetně té výpravy!) a zbytek filmu je zase totéž jako většina ostatních Marvel filmů: dvě-tři větší akce, trocha triviální filosofie o smyslu rodiny a přátelství, a na konci slib, že "v příštím pokračování to ale opravdu bude stát za to!" (Ilča 30 %)
